reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it presents a step-by-step educational discussion of YouTube monetization, including watch-time calculations and possible earnings from views. It does not describe a concrete offer requiring payment, credentials, or financial participation, and it frames sub-to-sub activity as against YouTube policy and something to avoid. The earnings discussion includes no guaranteed-return claim, required transaction, or stated pathway for transferring money or data.

Punta Kasta YouTube Studio and Ste Crater Studio. Pag Nandoung Kana, Kunta Ka Nandoung Samé Bandang Kaila, Eklik Mo Doon Sa Monetization.

opening.argument: Judge, the money claim is paired with a course of action. The video offers a step-by-step path to earning on YouTube, addresses people who want to start making videos, and tells them where to check progress toward the watch-time requirement. That makes the earnings discussion more than an isolated statistic: viewers are being guided to undertake the activity presented as the route to income. The absence of a payment request does not, by itself, resolve whether this is an income solicitation.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense's policy warning concerns sub-to-sub activity; it does not negate the separate invitation to consider making videos for earnings. Nor does the lack of a fee answer whether the title and instructions are trying to induce participation through an income prospect. The question is what the earnings discussion does in context, not only whether it requests money.

citations.quote: For those who want to start making videos on youtube and I also include how much you can earn in 1 million views to have the idea of ​​interested

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The cited action is making videos and checking one's own YouTube Studio watch time. Neither quote promises easy cash for completing a task or directs viewers into a claim, verification, or withdrawal flow. The description instead explains that only watch time within the last 365 days counts toward the requirement. An educational account of possible earnings is not evidence of a deceptive reward mechanism.

opening.argument: Judge, consider the combined effect of the money-focused title and the example of earnings from a million views. The description also walks through the 4,000-hour requirement and tells viewers how to check their count. Those details can make the income prospect feel concrete and attainable: an earnings figure is placed alongside a measurable milestone and a next step. That presentation deserves scrutiny even though it stops short of stating a guaranteed payout.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense correctly notes the warning against sub-to-sub activity, but that warning addresses one prohibited tactic, not the persuasive effect of the earnings example. Likewise, accurate instructions for finding watch time can lend credibility to an income pitch. The defense's absence-of-payment point leaves that framing unanswered.

citations.quote: It is against YouTube's policy and everyone should refrain from engaging in this kind of activity.
For those who want to start making videos on youtube and I also include how much you can earn in 1 million views to have the idea of ​​interested

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A million views is an example for discussing possible earnings, not a promised reward for an easy action. The description explicitly calls its watch-hours scenario an extreme example and explains why those hours would not count after 365 days. These qualifications undercut the suggestion of an assured or unusually easy payout; the cited milestone is a platform eligibility requirement, not a deceptive claim flow.

citations.quote: I just used an extreme example where your channel accumulated 3,999 hours a day and after that no one watched your channel again.
The 3,999 hours have been ignored because it has not been in the last 365 days so youTube will not count for a 4,000 -hour requirement.

opening.argument: Judge, the instructional form can itself serve a promotional purpose. The title leads with earning money, the description addresses prospective creators through a million-view earnings example, and the spoken directions move viewers into YouTube Studio's monetization area. Read together, this is not merely a detached explanation of a rule: it steers viewers toward pursuing the income opportunity being described. The policy disclaimer may make the presentation appear cautious, but it does not change that direction of travel.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense calls the Studio directions operational instruction, but that is also how a viewer is moved from interest in earnings toward checking monetization. The sub-to-sub warning distinguishes an impermissible tactic; it does not make the money-led framing neutral. A payment or credential request is not necessary to ask whether the tutorial promotes participation.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Guiding viewers to their own YouTube Studio monetization page is consistent with explaining eligibility. The opening identifies no separate product, claim site, payment, or reward offered for signing up. The description also expressly discourages sub-to-sub activity. Presenting information that may interest prospective creators does not establish a deceptive participation pathway.
